analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 15% minimum tax on the profits of America's largest corporations.
analysis.headline: The repeal bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act created a 15% minimum tax on the profits very large corporations report on their financial statements, making sure the biggest companies pay at least that much even if deductions and credits reduce their regular tax bill to near zero. This bill would erase that tax retroactively, treating it as if it had never been enacted. It was introduced in late September 2022, weeks before an election, and never received committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the repeal would benefit the small number of very large, highly profitable corporations that the minimum tax applies to — companies with roughly a billion dollars or more in average annual profits. It would take away the guarantee that these firms pay at least 15% of their financial-statement income in federal tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The largest and most profitable corporations

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 15% corporate alternative minimum tax that was enacted as part of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, applying as if that tax had never been written into law.

For the largest corporations, the minimum tax sets a floor on tax owed based on profits reported to shareholders, limiting how far deductions and credits can push their tax bill down; repeal removes that floor entirely, retroactively.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would lose the revenue the minimum tax raises — on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars over a decade — which would come out of deficit reduction and funding that accompanied the 2022 law. That cost is ultimately carried by taxpayers through larger deficits or reduced services.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the tax would forgo the substantial revenue it was projected to raise, weakening the deficit reduction that was part of the 2022 law's design.

Supporters of repeal argued that taxing financial-statement income rather than taxable income is poorly designed — it can apply to companies even when they owe little regular tax under existing rules, for example after large one-time losses — a fair objection that a well-drafted minimum tax could address with carve-outs rather than full repeal. (This objection is not documented in the provided sources.)

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow narrowly to a few dozen of the country's largest corporations, while the cost — hundreds of billions in forgone revenue over ten years — is spread across everyone through higher deficits. Repeal addresses a real design complaint about book-income taxes, but full retroactive repeal removes the only guarantee that the most profitable companies pay at least 15%. The bill also had no path forward: it was a single-party bill introduced weeks before the end of the Congress with no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from introduction until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 29, 2022, by Rep. Jodey Arrington with 12 Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee.
The tax it targeted — a 15% alternative minimum tax on corporations' financial-statement income — remained in law, having been enacted by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's interest in keeping the minimum tax intact was served by the bill's inaction: the largest corporations continue to owe at least 15% on their financial-statement profits, and the revenue tied to that tax was not given back. Large corporations would have been the clear winners had it passed, but the bill never advanced far enough to deliver anything.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers — the tax stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the corporate minimum tax on September 29, 2022.

for.name: 12 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the bill received no committee action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — 13 of the chamber's roughly 213 House Republicans — with no Democratic support, and the bill never advanced past the Ways and Means Committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Very large, highly profitable corporations (those subject to the $1 billion book minimum tax)
industries.note: Repeal would let the largest corporations escape the 15% floor on tax owed on their financial-statement profits, removing the guarantee that they pay a baseline amount even when deductions and credits cut their regular tax to near zero. The revenue they would avoid is money the rest of taxpayers would eventually cover through deficits or reduced services.
